01.note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda were sitting together when Geneiva passed by. One of them said they should stand for him, since he was a man of Torah; the other objected: should we stand for a quarrelsome man? Meanwhile Geneiva came over and asked what they were studying. When they said winds, he passed on a teaching of Rav: four winds blow every day and the north wind blows with each of them, or the world could not survive an hour; the south wind is the harshest, and it would destroy the whole world if the angel Ben Netz did not hold it back.
01.why: The Gemara has been explaining the harsh east wind of Jonah and how the south wind silences the other winds; this encounter carries the theme of the winds further.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav Hisda; one of the two debates whether to stand for Geneiva.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rav Huna when Geneiva passes.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: A learned man whom one of the Sages calls quarrelsome; he joins them and teaches about the winds.

people.name: Ben Netz
people.about: An angel who, in the teaching Geneiva cites, holds back the south wind.

terms.meaning: A Torah scholar. Standing up when a scholar passes is a mark of respect, which is why the two Sages debate whether Geneiva deserves it.

02.note: Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak were sitting when Rav Nahman bar Yaakov rode by in a gilded carriage under a green cloak. Rava went over to him; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak stayed put, saying the riders were probably the Exilarch's people, whom Rava needed and he did not. When he saw who it was, he went over too. Rav Nahman bar Yaakov bared his arm and said the wind called Shadya was blowing. Rava cited Rav that a woman miscarries in that wind, Shmuel that even a pearl in the sea rots, and Rabbi Yohanan that even the seed in a woman's womb putrefies. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak pointed out that all three drew their teaching from a single verse in Hosea.
02.why: The Gemara is gathering teachings about winds, after Geneiva's account of the four winds. Right after this, Rava praises Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak as a man of Sura, where they are precise with verses.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who goes to greet Rav Nahman bar Yaakov at once and cites Rav on the Shadya wind.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who at first does not go over, thinking the riders are the Exilarch's people; he ties the three teachings to one verse.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who rides by in a gilded carriage and remarks that the Shadya wind is blowing.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful official with his own household and court.
The name of a hot, harmful wind; the Sages here describe the damage it causes.

03.note: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled that he was one of five elders sitting before Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha. A man came before Rabbi Yoshiya, who compelled him, against his will, to authorize a bill of divorce. Rabbi Yoshiya then told the elders: go and hide, and write the bill of divorce for her.
03.why: The Gemara wants to know which rulings follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and which follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in two disputes about cancelling a bill of divorce. It infers from the order to hide, rather than to scatter, that Rabbi Yoshiya followed one of them in each.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who tells this as an eyewitness, one of the five elders present.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya from Usha
people.about: The Sage who compels the man to authorize the divorce and tells the elders to hide while writing it.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband must have written and delivered to his wife to end a marriage. A husband may try to cancel it before it reaches her.

04.note: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent a bill of divorce to his wife. The messenger found her sitting and weaving and told her: here is your bill of divorce. She said: at least go away for now and come back tomorrow. The messenger went back and told Giddul, who responded with the blessing: Blessed is He Who is good and does good. Abaye said that Giddul blessed God but the bill of divorce was still valid; Rava said that he blessed God and the bill of divorce was cancelled.
04.why: The Gemara has been discussing how a husband can cancel a bill of divorce he has sent. It explains that Abaye and Rava disagree over whether a husband merely showing that he no longer wants it delivered cancels it.

people.name: Giddul bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who sends his wife a bill of divorce and then blesses God when it is not delivered.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who holds that the bill of divorce stays valid.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who holds that the bill of divorce is cancelled.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that ends a marriage once it is delivered to the wife; until then the husband may cancel it.

terms.term: Blessed is He Who is good and does good
terms.meaning: A blessing said on hearing good news. The translation explains that Giddul said it because he was glad the divorce had not been delivered.

05.note: Rav Sheshet compelled a certain man, against his will, to authorize a bill of divorce. The man then told the witnesses: this is what Rav Sheshet says to you, let the bill of divorce be cancelled. Rav Sheshet made him authorize another bill of divorce.
05.why: Rava cites this case to prove his view that a husband's showing he does not want the divorce cancels it. Abaye answers that the man had really cancelled it himself, and only blamed Rav Sheshet to avoid being flogged.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who forces a man to divorce his wife and then requires a second bill of divorce.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that ends a marriage. Witnesses write or sign it on the husband's instruction, and he can cancel it before it is delivered.

06.note: Rav Yehuda compelled the son-in-law of Rabbi Yirmeya Bira'a to authorize a bill of divorce, and the man cancelled it. Rav Yehuda compelled him again, and again he cancelled it. The third time Rav Yehuda compelled him against his will and told the witnesses: stuff gourd in your ears and write it for him. The man ran after the witnesses, but they could not hear him.
06.why: Abaye cites this case to prove that a husband merely showing he does not want the divorce does not cancel it: the witnesses could see him chasing them. Rava replies he might have been running to tell them to hurry.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who forces the man to divorce three times and has the witnesses block their ears.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya Bira'a
people.about: A Sage whose son-in-law is being compelled to divorce his wife.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that ends a marriage. A husband can cancel it by saying so before witnesses, which is why the witnesses here block their ears.

07.note: A man who was betrothed told witnesses: if I do not marry her within thirty days, let this be a bill of divorce. When the thirty days came, he told them: I tried, but could not. The text does not say what became of the divorce.
07.why: The Gemara asks what doubt there could be: circumstances beyond a man's control do not count for a bill of divorce, and if his words show he no longer wants it, that is the dispute of Abaye and Rava, where the ruling follows Abaye.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic law a couple was first betrothed, which already bound them as husband and wife, and only later married; ending a betrothal required a bill of divorce.
The document, called a get, that ends a marriage or a betrothal. A man could give one on a condition, so that it takes effect only if the condition is not met.

08.note: During years of famine a man left a gold dinar for safekeeping with a widow. She put it in a jar of flour, unknowingly baked it into a loaf of bread, and gave the loaf to a poor man. Some time later the owner came and asked for his dinar. She swore: may poison take hold of one of my children if I benefited at all from your dinar. Within a few days one of her children died. When the Sages heard, they said: if this happens to one who swears truthfully, how much more to one who swears falsely.
08.why: The mishna says courts stopped making widows swear an oath to collect their marriage payment. The Gemara asks whether this incident, showing how dangerous an oath is, was the reason, and then asks why it would apply only to widows.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who reports this incident in the name of Rav; some say it was Rav Yehuda.

terms.meaning: A coin; a gold dinar was worth a good deal of money.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and explains, line by line.

09.note: A widow came before Rav Huna to collect her marriage payment. He told her: what can I do for you, since Rav does not collect a marriage payment for a widow. She answered: isn't the only reason the worry that I already took some of it? As the Lord of Hosts lives, I have not benefited from my marriage contract at all. Rav Huna said: Rav agrees in the case of a woman who jumps in and swears of her own accord.
09.why: The Gemara has explained that Rav would not let widows collect, because the courts no longer had them swear and vows were taken lightly. Rav Huna's ruling carves out an exception to Rav's practice.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A judge who at first refuses the widow, citing Rav, then accepts her oath.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rav Huna's authority, who did not collect marriage payments for widows.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money if her husband dies or divorces her. A widow collects it from her late husband's estate, which now belongs to his heirs.
A woman who takes an oath on her own initiative, without the court asking her to.

10.note: A widow came before Rav Huna, who said he could not collect her marriage payment because Rav did not; she swore of her own accord that she had taken nothing, and Rav Huna ruled that Rav agrees in such a case. Another widow came before Rav Huna's son, Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told her that neither Rav nor his own father collected a marriage payment for a widow. She asked him at least to give her support. He said she had no right to that either, citing Shmuel: a widow who demands her marriage payment in court loses her support. She said: let his chair be overturned, he has treated me by the rulings of two different people. He overturned his chair and set it up again, and even so he was not spared from weakness.
10.why: The Gemara has explained Rav's refusal to let widows collect their marriage payment. Next, Rav Yehuda, Shmuel's student, tells a judge to find ways to let widows collect, against the practice of Rav's students.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A judge who follows Rav's practice but accepts a widow's oath taken of her own accord; father of Rabba bar Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who refuses a widow both her marriage payment and her support, and is struck by her curse.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling, that a widow who sues for her marriage payment loses her support, Rabba bar Rav Huna cites.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money if her husband dies or divorces her; a widow collects it from his estate.
Food and support a widow may draw from her late husband's estate as long as she has not claimed her marriage payment.

11.note: A certain teacher of young children was negligent with them. Rav Aha made him take a vow, with the community's consent, to stop teaching. Later Ravina reinstated him, because no one else could be found who was as careful in teaching as he was.
11.why: Ameimar ruled that a vow taken with the community's consent cannot be released. The Gemara limits this to vows about optional matters: for the sake of a commandment it can be released, as with this teacher.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: The Sage who has the negligent teacher vow, with the community's consent, to stop teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who reinstates the teacher when no equally careful teacher can be found.

terms.term: vow on the consent of the public
terms.meaning: A vow whose terms depend on the community's agreement. Normally a Sage can release a person from a vow, but such a vow was held to be harder to undo.
A commandment or religious duty. Teaching children Torah counts as one.

12.note: A relative of Rabbi Asi held a loan document that included a guarantee on the borrower's property. He asked Rabbi Asi whether the Sabbatical Year cancels the debt, and was told it does not. He then went to Rabbi Yohanan, who said it does. Rabbi Asi came and asked Rabbi Yohanan himself, who again said it does. Rabbi Asi protested that Rabbi Yohanan himself had said it does not. Rabbi Yohanan replied: just because that is how we reason, should we act on it? When Rabbi Asi pointed to a teaching that supports him, Rabbi Yohanan answered that perhaps it follows Beit Shammai, who hold that a document waiting to be collected counts as already collected.
12.why: The Gemara has set out a dispute over whether the Sabbatical Year cancels loans backed by a property guarantee, with Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish saying it does not. This case shows Rabbi Yohanan refusing to rule by his own view in practice.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage who rules for his relative that the debt stands, then questions Rabbi Yohanan about his contrary ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Rabbi Asi's teacher, who rules that the debt is cancelled, even though he had reasoned otherwise.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when by Torah law outstanding loans are cancelled and lenders may no longer demand repayment.
A clause in a loan document pledging the borrower's land as security, so the lender can collect from it.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the main collection of their teachings.
The school of the early Sage Shammai, whose rulings are generally not followed in practice.

12.flag: The first STORY segment is a baraita stating the law, not part of the narrative; the story begins at the second STORY segment.

13.note: Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Minyumi, owed Rabba money. He brought it to him during the Sabbatical Year, and Rabba said: I cancel the debt. Abba took the money and left. Abaye found Rabba sad, and Rabba told him what had happened. Abaye went to Abba and asked whether he had answered: nevertheless, take it. Abba said no. Abaye told him that if he had, Rabba would have taken it, so he should bring it back now and say so. Abba did, and Rabba took the money. Rabba said: this young scholar had no sense to begin with.
13.why: The mishna says a lender paid in the Sabbatical Year must say he cancels the debt, but may accept if the borrower says: nevertheless. Rabba has just ruled the lender may hopefully wait for those words, and here he does.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also called Abba bar Minyumi; a young scholar who owes Rabba money and takes Rabba's words literally.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The lender, who formally cancels the debt and is saddened when the borrower takes him at his word.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who notices Rabba's sadness and coaches the borrower on what to say.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when by Torah law outstanding loans are cancelled; a lender may accept repayment only if the borrower insists.
The formal words, I cancel the debt, that a lender must say when a borrower offers repayment in the Sabbatical Year.

14.note: Shmuel's maidservant was taken captive. Some people ransomed her as a maidservant and sent her back to him with a message: we follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and even if you follow the Rabbis, we ransomed her as a maidservant. The Gemara adds that they thought this happened before Shmuel had given up hope of getting her back, but in fact it was after. So Shmuel not only did not keep her as a slave; he did not even require her to receive a writ of freedom.
14.why: The mishna disputes whether a slave ransomed from captivity stays a slave, and the Gemara asks whether that depends on the owner having given up hope. Shmuel acts on his own view that a slave whose owner renounces him is free without a document.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Called Master Shmuel; his maidservant is captured and ransomed, and he treats her as a free woman.

terms.meaning: An owner's giving up hope of recovering something lost or taken. After that point the law can treat the item, or here the slave, as no longer his.
A writ of freedom: the document a master gives a slave to set him or her free.

terms.term: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis
terms.meaning: The two sides of the mishna's dispute over whether a slave ransomed from captivity remains a slave or goes free.

15.note: The maidservant of Rabbi Abba bar Zutra was taken captive, and a gentile ransomed her to be his wife. The Sages sent word to Rabbi Abba bar Zutra: if you want to do the right thing, send her a writ of freedom. The text does not say what he did.
15.why: The Gemara asks what a writ of freedom could achieve. It answers that the townspeople would then ransom her as a free Jewish woman, or that her captor would think less of her as a Jew's maidservant and let her be ransomed.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Zutra
people.about: A Sage whose maidservant is captured; the Sages advise him to free her.

terms.meaning: A writ of freedom: the document a master gives a slave to set him or her free.
A word the translation leaves untranslated; it describes the man as a gentile.

16.note: In Pumbedita there was a maidservant with whom men were committing forbidden sexual acts. Abaye said that, were it not for Shmuel's teaching that anyone who frees his slave violates a commandment, he would force her master to write her a writ of freedom. Ravina said that in a case like this one, even Shmuel's student Rav Yehuda agrees, because of the forbidden acts.
16.why: The Gemara is discussing when a slave may be freed. It goes on to challenge Abaye from a case where a court forced a master to free a half-slave woman, then distinguishes the two.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who would force the master to free her, if not for the teaching against freeing slaves.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who holds that freeing her is allowed in such a case.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who passes on Shmuel's teaching that freeing a slave violates a commandment.

terms.meaning: A commandment to do something. Shmuel reads the verse about keeping slaves forever as such a commandment, so freeing a slave breaks it.
A writ of freedom: the document a master gives a slave to set her free, after which she could marry a Jew.

17.note: In Pumbedita men were committing forbidden sexual acts with a certain maidservant. Abaye said that, were it not for Shmuel's teaching that freeing a slave violates a commandment, he would force her master to free her; Ravina said that in such a case even Rav Yehuda agrees she may be freed. The Gemara then recalls an incident told by Rabbi Yitzhak: a woman who was half maidservant and half free, whose master the court forced to set her fully free. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak explained that men had been treating her as if she belonged to no one.
17.why: The Gemara uses the half-free woman's case to ask whether Abaye really rejects freeing a slave to prevent sin. It answers that the cases differ: she could marry neither a slave nor a free man, while a full maidservant can be given to a slave who will guard her.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who would force the Pumbedita master to free his maidservant, if not for the teaching against freeing slaves.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who holds that freeing her is allowed because of the forbidden acts.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who explains why the court forced the half-free woman's master to free her.

terms.meaning: A woman owned by two masters, one of whom had freed his share of her, leaving her half free.
A commandment to do something. Shmuel reads the verse about keeping slaves forever as such a commandment.

17.flag: The span joins the Pumbedita maidservant case with the Gemara's objection that cites a separate incident (a half-free woman); the Pumbedita case alone is also its own story.

18.note: Rabbi Eliezer entered a synagogue and did not find the ten men needed for prayer. So he freed his slave, and the slave completed the ten.
18.why: Shmuel taught that freeing a slave violates a commandment. The Gemara raises Rabbi Eliezer's act as an objection and answers that freeing a slave for the sake of a commandment is different.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who frees his slave so that there will be ten men for prayer.

terms.meaning: The ten adult Jewish men needed for public prayer. A slave did not count toward it, but a freed slave did.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the main collection of their teachings.

19.note: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak found Rava bar She'eilta standing at the door of a house of prayer and asked whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rava bar She'eilta said: I say it does not, but the Sages who came from Mehoza report, in the name of Rav Nahman, that it does. The account goes on: when the speaker came to Sura, he asked Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin what had actually happened. He was told that a maidservant whose master lay dying came crying to him: how long will that woman stay enslaved? The master took his hat, threw it to her, and said: go acquire this, and acquire yourself. When they came before Rav Nahman, he said: he has done nothing.
19.why: Rabbi Shimon holds that a slave is freed only by a writ, not by payment, and the Sages disagree whether the law follows him. Next, the Gemara says Rav Nahman's ruling here did not rest on that view, but on the master having used his own hat for the transfer.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who asks whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rava bar She'eilta
people.about: A Sage, found at the door of a house of prayer, who answers and reports what others say.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin
people.about: A Sage in Sura who tells what actually happened in the case Rav Nahman ruled on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who rules that the dying master's act did not free the maidservant.

terms.meaning: Jewish law as it is actually practised; asking whether the halakha follows a Sage means asking whether his view is the binding one.
A way of transferring ownership by handing over an object; the master tried to give the maidservant ownership of herself by having her take his hat.

20.note: A town of slaves had been sold to gentiles. When their last gentile owners died, the slaves came before Ravina. He told them: go back to the children of your first owners and have them write you writs of freedom. The Sages objected that Ameimar had said a slave whose master renounced him and died has no remedy. Ravina answered that he followed Rav Dimi's report. They said Rav Dimi's report was mistaken. Ravina replied: mistaken only in that the master had not used words of freeing; had he used them, it would hold.
20.why: The Gemara has just recorded Ameimar and Rav Ashi debating whether a renounced slave can still be freed and whether Rav Dimi's report is mistaken. This case puts that debate into practice, and the Gemara rules like Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who tells the slaves to get writs of freedom from their first owners' children, and defends that ruling.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage whose ruling, that a renounced slave whose master has died has no remedy, the Sages raise against Ravina.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage whose report of Rabbi Yohanan's ruling Ravina relies on.

terms.meaning: A town or estate, here one whose people were slaves.
A writ of freedom: the document a master, or his heirs, gives a slave to set him free and let him live as a full Jew.
Words that actually declare a slave free, as opposed to a looser instruction about how heirs should treat the slave.
